Q: Strategy to manage multiple apps with common features A:

If the common features do not affect the API between services you can just develop an internal library, deployed with nuget, that is used by all the services. If services happen to use different versions it should not be a significant issue since the APIs remain the same.

If these common features do affect the APIs, are you sure microservices are the best solution for your particular problem? A core tenet of microservices is independence and independent deployability. This makes changes in the APIs between services intentionally very costly, since services are required to maintain old APIs for some time. If the common features are placed in a library each service would need to simultaneously use multiple versions of that library to maintain the old APIs, and that sound very difficult and costly to me. And that assumes all services even use the same language.

Microservices mostly benefit very large organizations with hundreds of developers. If you are that large, should you not ask your colleges instead? If not, are you sure that independent deployability is worth the cost? Perhaps it is better to design a more conventional application that is deployed all at once? All at once deployment makes your problem so much easier since you can just use a common library. The project may still use separate services where it make sense, but it is perfectly possible to keep a clean separation between components in a single application, see "modular monolith". And modern servers should provide plenty of vertical scaling if needed.

Q: How to ask Android for the right to access user files A:

pick_dir() is not a permission request. It opens Android's SAF folder picker.

Your code is probably not showing anything because you're calling it during DOMContentLoaded. On Android, these dialogs usually need to be triggered by a direct user action (button click, menu tap, etc).

Also, modern Android does not allow normal apps to get unrestricted access to /storage/emulated/0 anymore. With SAF, the user grants access only to the folder they select, not the whole storage.

So your Rust code is mostly fine. Try invoking it from a button click instead of automatically on startup.

Q: Godot - Detecting a new Area3D completely inside existing Area3D A:

Ah! I see. And whenever someone dies, in this case, you spawn this area3D to mark the evidence so that any NPC that finds it can act accordingly.
Hm.. I assume there's all kinds of possible events you eventually will have (or already have) so doing an overlapping check is most likely the cheapest way to keep every behavior working as it is right now, with the addition that it will work when something happens "in-sight" as well.

A more design focused question would be, should the NPCs behave the same in both scenarios? As in the following:

if an NPC stumbles upon a corpse, I'd assume the NPC would get alerted and curious, so it would approach and investigate. But if a murder happens within their sight technically it already should "know" what happened, since they witnessed it, so the behavior is different.

If this is the case, you could instead of using the same event logic you have now (with the overlap addition) build a separate system that tracks known states of "things" the NPC knows about and acts when a state of something they know about changes.

For instance, if another NPC is in their sight, you'd add that to their immediate memory. so the NPC would have 1 tracked "entity" that is of type NPC. Once the character dies, its state has changed and you could, instead of triggering the eventArea3D, listen to this state change signal and iterate through all NPCs within a region to see if they have this other NPC in their memory, if they do, that means they had it in sight and should act in a certain way.

This enables all sorts of combinations, depending on the agents and what they can know about other agents. If that's something you'd want, then it's something worth looking into, if the area3D trigger is enough, then the AABB check should suffice :)

Q: Document AI: distinguish between a "0" and an "O" A:

You're asking about OCR, not AI. OCR already do this since the 1990s.

OCR software handles this for decades using AI algorithms- it was already pretty good in the late 1990s, a lot better in the early 2000s. And of course, the commercial versions of each application or service were better than the free ones. Even for cloud services like Azure Vision, the free tier is worse than paid tiers, because both the algorithms and the available hardware are less powerful.

OCR doesn't just recognize individual characters, it looks at words, takes into account the language, recognizes the document layout, so it can use different algorithms for prose and eg billing codes. They also take into account the business domain, as doctors will use different vocabulary compared to lawyers, engineers or the general public. After the initial scan, possibly transparent to the user, spell checking is used to correct errors. Also statistical analysis to detect unexpected results that probably need correcting.

There's no single "AI" to train, there are a lot of relevant algorithms used together. Many of them are statistical, like Hidden Markov Models. I'm still talking about the 90s-00s.

The OCR companies collected and scanned a lot of documents across different domains in the 1990s-2000s to build and train their software. They also created language models, spell checkers that would detect and correct errors.

As for on a PDF it might be written as "AB00012, you may not need OCR at all. Unless the file contains a photo (in which case it's not really a PDF), the characters are in the file. A PDF is a file containing printing instructions in PostScript, eg go to coordinates X,Y, print text "ABO0012" using Times New Roman, 12 points in red. Unfortunately, the commands can be in any order, Eg printing from back to forth, top down. You need to know how the printed/rendered document actually looks, which is why OCR can be used on the rendered output.

BUT if you already have the instructions, you can use them along with the rendered image to understand what's what.

Again, you're more likely to find such functionality in commercial products and services.

PS: For unstructured text, you can use Named Entity Recognition algorithms try to determine what each part of unstructured text is so you can use different rules on it. At the very least, you can use such algorithms for corrections.

Googling for OCR and Named Entity Recognition I see the combinatino is now a separate area called Visual NLP. I also see results mentioning common language processing libraries like spaCy, which already offers NER. Some of the results are blog posts using both OCR and NER tools, eg Tesseract for OCR, spaCy for NER.
